rows.source_grounded_reason: Le Chapelier and the triumvirs turn from radical attack to consolidation; collaboration with Lafayette and the constitutional settlement fail to secure aristocratic, provincial-club and Paris-press support.

Religious controversy and the Jalès alarm enlarge provincial Jacobin activity. Varennes prompts mobilization and deposition demands, but republican commitment is limited; Paris Jacobins divide over monarchy.
Émigré planners interpret southern Catholic militancy as a restoration opportunity; Lyon and Jalès schemes fail amid weak coordination and unreliable assessments.
Troop concentration and Necker’s dismissal interact with scarcity, arming, militia formation and Guards’ defection; the Bastille is an escalation within this July sequence.
The oath and enforcement of religious changes draw local Catholics into resistance beyond noble émigrés. Sectarian and local grievances must not be equated with uniform Bourbon commitment.

Mirabeau hoped to stabilize the revolutionary monarchy and shares some escape tactics with royalists without sharing their restoration objective. His advice is covered by the coherent Mirabeau task 55; Varennes consequences are separate.
Administrative reform was defensible in its aims, but unilateral lay restructuring and the oath ruptured authority and religious confidence; the whole preceding Church sequence exceeds this task.
Elected courts lack administrative and police power, authorities depend on uneven National Guards, and tax reform is adopted without effective compulsory collection machinery.
Robespierre’s antislavery rhetoric contrasts with Barnave’s colonial compromise and the Assembly’s limited free-coloured rights; these are distinct from Robespierre’s procedural ascent.

Verification becomes a struggle over representation and national legitimacy, culminating in the unilateral National Assembly. It does not require every political precursor and later Guard institution.

The sequence distinguishes limited and then full free-coloured rights, slave revolt, local emancipation, Convention abolition, and Haitian resistance to restoration. Colonial war and disease qualify simple metropolitan causation.

Publicity, pamphlets, clubs, petitions and provincial conflict shift the struggle from resistance to ministerial despotism toward attacks on privilege; later Bastille events are not necessary parts of this specific question.

Doyle dates counter-revolution to resistance to national sovereignty, not all earlier reform opposition. Most Federalists defend republican representation; Toulon’s later conditional royalism is a qualified exception.
Popular force makes July and October victories possible, while property-conscious deputies restrict citizenship and authorize Guard coercion. Dependence and exclusion are a source tension.
The memory of Law’s collapse and distrust of financiers defeat bank proposals, favor visibly secured national-land paper, and recur in the Directory’s rejection of a land-backed bank.

Universal rights and exile advocacy internationalize expectations, but European powers remain divided and intervention conditional; Varennes changes perceptions without immediately producing a united crusade.
Barnave’s acceptance of slavery and narrowly qualified rights for free people of colour must be distinguished from complete political or racial equality.
Cadoudal gains relative standing after Quiberon and continues conspiracy after much of the west is pacified; he does not establish unified control over all chouans.

Equal and supposedly humane execution becomes a Terror symbol. Its famous Paris victims are not representative of the mainly provincial death toll; colonial emancipation is unrelated to the retrieval demand.
Suspicion of arbitrary power separates functions and weakens the executive while excluding the courts from administration; judicial reconstruction is essential to this institutional comparison.

Civilian shortages, paper collapse and land speculation juxtapose misery with conspicuous fortunes, reopen radical political space and produce popular nostalgia for the Terror; this is not an endorsement of Babeuf’s programme.
Hoche combines military pressure with religious accommodation and restraint of republican abuses; negotiated peace is uneven and renewed resistance is not simply defeated by force alone.

The Assembly defies the Royal Session; popular pressure and Guards’ refusal make enforcement uncertain. Clergy and forty-seven nobles join before the king orders union on 27 June; later July withdrawal is a different event.
The law grows from labour conflict and political consolidation; its suppression of collective worker organization lasts far beyond the immediate strike emergency.

Different fiscal devices follow one another but have different effects: inflation, failed mandates, default, administrative collection and banking reconstruction. Stabilization is qualified, not an automatic result of abolishing paper.
Avignon and the Comtat tie papal temporal sovereignty to revolutionary annexation and intensify conflict with Rome; this is not the same demand as all European intervention fears.

The king’s declaration repudiates the settlement, but deputies retain monarchy and use the kidnapping fiction because constitutional stability and fear of popular power outweigh a republican alternative.
Abolition of venal justice creates elected and free courts while the property principle requires office-holder compensation, enlarging debt and driving assignat issue.
Lafayette organizes the Paris Guard yet is subject to pressure from his own troops, as October reveals; federation adds public prestige without erasing uncertain discipline.

Foreign responses range from enthusiasm to hostility and polarized debate; British and German reactions are not a single European progression, and Varennes strengthens fears without uniform intervention.
Puisaye’s claims overstate fragmented chouan strength and coordination, shaping British expectations for an expedition that lacks the promised united support.
Robespierre’s republican commitment remains uncertain amid opposition to elite settlement; procedural and rhetorical radicalism should not be converted into unequivocal republican intent.
Religious schism, coercion, royal repudiation, popular repression and failed elite consolidation dismantle the apparent consensus; these are connected causes, not interchangeable meanings.

Early leadership is socially and politically diverse: Sieyes, Mirabeau, Breton organization, Orléans patronage and third-estate cohesion perform distinct roles. This does not require every later constitutional turning point.

Private property rights justify compensation for venal offices and redemption for feudal dues, while tithes are abolished outright and corporate Church assets are appropriated. The different property claims must remain explicit.
Catholic resistance at Nîmes and gatherings at Jalès encourage royalist expectations, but local conflict does not become a reliably directed restoration army.
The Assembly’s colonial exception protects slavery against universal rights rhetoric; limited rights for free people of colour do not amount to slave emancipation.
Maximum repeal responds to discredit and market preferences; winter, harvest, transport, fuel and army demand combine with printing and inflation to produce famine and shrinking Paris rations.

Sieyes supplies a constitutional strategy, Mirabeau and journalism exploit publicity, and galleries and Palais Royal mobilization pressure representatives; their roles are complementary rather than identical.

The 1793 constitution is ratified but suspended, then becomes an insurgent rallying point and is rejected as unworkable. Louis XVII’s death and Verona close agreement with the Convention, not all future electoral monarchy.
Veto, assembly preponderance and indirect property-qualified suffrage limit executive action and political participation; the September revisions preserve some exclusions while changing others.

Women participate on opposing religious sides: Catholic mobilization in the south and attacks on refractory worship in Paris. Political action should not be collapsed into a single republican movement.
The Day of Daggers exposes Lafayette’s insecurity on both court and popular fronts; collaboration with the triumvirs later seeks to secure a final constitutional settlement.
Army discipline and noble officer loyalties are destabilized, and post-Varennes oaths and emigration weaken the constitutional settlement; this is distinct from Guard organization.
Religious objections, confinement and the flight manifesto expose royal alienation; acceptance of the completed constitution is qualified by insincerity and hopes beyond it.
Delay, recognition and interrupted military protection defeat the flight. Doyle leaves uncertain what the king would do after reaching Montmédy; the uncertainty must remain explicit.

Loss of elite and Church demand, disrupted credit, paper overissue and colonial war harm the economy; war industries and cotton gain, while agriculture expands with population but retains inertia and land-oriented investment.
Foreign allies subordinate restoration to their own strategic interests; British cooperation depends on military utility and constitutional expectations rather than unconditional Bourbon loyalty.
The revised press regime criminalizes attacks on the constitution and incitement, revealing limits within the liberal settlement rather than a wholesale end of publicity.
National lands secure assignats and the Extraordinary Fund links land sales and debt redemption; the notes evolve from interest-bearing claims to currency with enlarged issue.
Conservative revisions consolidate the Assembly’s work but do not restore the full monarchien model; institutional achievements coexist with exclusion, weak authority and absent consensus.
Free-coloured political equality and emancipation of slaves occur by different decisions under different pressures; they are not interchangeable forms of abolition.
The blocked Saint-Cloud journey is evidence of royal confinement and a catalyst to escape planning, but Doyle does not identify it as a proven attempted flight.
Noble officers are suspected of royal loyalty and rank discipline is crumbling; patriots therefore depend on citizen Guards even though their discipline is also unreliable.
Mirabeau’s secret advice aims to stabilize a reformed monarchy; similar escape tactics do not make his objectives identical to émigré restoration.
Varennes turns emigration into a military enterprise and exposes factional friction; Valmy discredits and disperses much of it, while Condé’s force survives as a qualified exception.
Émigré centres, princely appeals and military recruitment operate amid Austrian caution, conditional declarations, rival Russian priorities and exceptional Swedish belligerence.
Citizen force and mass mobilization develop into military power capable of guaranteeing and coercing political regimes. Neither levée nor Brumaire is simple unanimous national consent.
Separation of judicial and administrative authority leaves public order with local administrators and their National Guards, without an independently provided police force.
Guard action varies across sectarian conflicts, royal movement, Lafayette’s insecurity and repression. Local composition and political pressure prevent a single consistent political role.
Persecution of nonjuring worship collides with proclaimed religious liberty and deepens division; doctrinal disagreement is not the whole explanation.

Depreciation undermines the state as payer and receiver; unsuccessful levies and rejected banking alternatives precede rapidly devalued mandates. Demonetization ends inflation but scarcity of coin causes deflation and barter.
Pillnitz is public menace with restrictive conditions and hesitant Austrian intentions; émigré exploitation and French fears exceed the immediate military commitment.

Robespierre’s motions excluding deputies from ministerial office and reelection gain a reputation for disinterestedness and obstruct rivals. His colonial position and republican uncertainty are separate inquiries.
Pius initially acts privately and cautiously, then condemns the settlement publicly and encourages retractions; papal policy helps harden a conflict already created in France.
Favras’s conspiracy has no demonstrated Turin coordination and ambiguous connections with Provence; the king’s public avowal of the Revolution deepens émigré anger.

After Varennes, deposition demands exceed settled republican conviction. Cordelier and Social Circle agitation, Jacobin division, the Feuillant exit and Champ de Mars repression form the coherent domestic sequence.
Electoral and militia struggles and fears for Catholic institutions mobilize southern crowds and invite royalist hopes; religious resistance is rooted in local confessional conflict.

Public oath choices divide clergy and communities; geography and social relations explain differences, new constitutional personnel face uneven authority, and papal condemnation stimulates retractions.
Removal of the silver mark opens deputy eligibility while higher secondary-elector qualifications retain an indirect property filter; the two levels must not be conflated.
Rank unrest and Nancy reveal conflicting military loyalties; Bouillé’s repression earns trust for the escape project but does not guarantee a successful rescue.
Municipal militias become a national institution combining public initiative, coercion and federation, with class qualification and uneven discipline.

Revenue collapse and resistance persist despite reformed taxes lacking effective enforcement; inherited debt and compensation for abolished offices enlarge obligations, driving nationalization and assignats.

Armed restoration fails through divided leadership, unrealistic aims, dependence on self-interested allies and popular hostility or exhaustion. Limited monarchy can still attract constitutional electoral support.
The Constituent’s 1789 ban on deputies becoming ministers for three years after departure differs from Robespierre’s four-year proposal in 1791. Keep the first rule’s institutional setting explicit.

The conscription crisis combines religious, local and social grievances. Weakly controlled Vendée towns permit a field army; better-garrisoned Brittany encourages dispersed guerrillas. Only the literal caption on 225 is eligible.
Necker’s return restores parlements but exposes disagreement over representation and head voting; the electoral framework becomes a renewed conflict rather than a financial settlement.
The Monarchical Club uses cheap bread to attract support but is attacked and fails; its philanthropic tactic is distinct from the later Feuillant organization.
Mallet du Pan advocates realistic constitutional restoration while d’Antraigues supplies factional intelligence and plots; networks can amplify division rather than coherence.
Rational legal and administrative institutions survive, but participation remains unequal and property, gender and stronger state control limit universal emancipation.
Champ de Mars converts republican petitioning into coercive confrontation; the disputed scale and political consequences of repression matter to constitutional consolidation.

Quiberon fails through confused command, unreliable recruits and coordination, and Hoche’s containment; the Yeu project is immobilized by control of the coast rather than defeated in the same fashion.

Princely restoration retains privileged-order assumptions and contradicts moderate constitutional monarchism. Verona hardens refusal; the source’s 13 June/23 June dating discrepancy must be qualified.

Condé’s surviving force and contacts with Pichegru connect military subversion to restoration; earlier Lyon organization and the later conspiracy are different stages, not proof of one coherent network.
The Tennis Court commitment claims national constituent authority, while the Royal Session grants reforms within a crown-centred order and protected privileges; deputies refuse the king’s settlement.

Corporate clerical wealth and services are damaged, but papal spiritual authority revives. The Concordat secures religion and new property while appointments and Organic Articles impose state control; long-term conflict persists.
The cockade fuses royal white with Paris colours and is adopted by the king; perceived insults to it help politicize the October crisis.
